We often see news articles about the results of a study, so what is a study anyway?
Im guessing a study involves a lot more paperwork. Hypothesis, Experiment, conclusion, publish in scientific journals. Maybe request a grant before or after.
Did you not go to school bro? A study is an experiment that is examined and studied.

This is actually a lot deeper of a question than it seems at first. "A study" can mean anything from a feasibility study that you have an engineering summer intern bang out on whatever you feel like to a published Nature article with scores of postdoc contributors. Essentially it means a systematic examination of a specific topic. It's always important to exam the academic credibility of any "study", most importantly the source it was published in. (Roughly high impact journals like Nature or Materials Today go to the front of the list; trade publications like Aviation Week & Space Technology or Institute of Transportation Engineers Journal come next; popular science literature for the uninitiated like Popular Mechanics got to the bottom of the list; things like Fox/MSNBC propaganda go directly in the garbage and are not to be considered.) The next most important thing to consider is the author, so the research team and institution. (A study at Oxford where the department chair was also the PI will go to the top of the list above nowhere Oklahoma's PhD candidates.) Methodology is very important, but difficult to critique if you're not an expert in the field so we generally rely on the first two. You can also talk about things like Erdos number or wank around with other metrics about citations.

TLDR: A "study" can mean whatever the person trying to sell it to you wants it to mean. The most important thing is to always think critically about what they're trying to sell you on, mainly who performed it, how, and who published their findings.
